title: The hash ring: adding or removing a database without moving everything
dek: Follow one system from a single database to several. Splitting match data across databases with hash % N works until a database is added or lost; then nearly everything moves. Putting databases and keys on a ring limits the move to one slice, and giving each database many points on the ring spreads that slice evenly. Every step here is one you can draw on a whiteboard.

items: Modulo hashing (hash(id) % 3) is simple and even, but going to % 4 or % 2 changes the home of almost every key.
On a ring, each key belongs to the first database clockwise from its hash. Adding a database moves only the keys between it and its neighbour; removing one moves only its own keys.
One point per database leaves the ring uneven, and a failed database dumps all its keys on one neighbour. Many virtual points per database spread both the data and the failures evenly.

body.x: Picture the ticketing side of a cricket app. At first it is simple: one database holds every match, its seats and its bookings, and the app servers read from it. It works well, until the app gets popular, hosts every league and tour, and one database can't keep up. The data has to be split across several databases, which is sharding, and that raises one question: which database holds which match?

body.cap: One database for every match works until it doesn't. Split across three, every request first needs to know which database holds its match.

body.x: The obvious rule: hash the match id to a number, take it modulo the number of databases, and the result is the database.

body.label: Modulo hashing over three databases
body.x:
database = hash(match_id) % 3

match 1234 → hash(1234) % 3 = 1 → database 1
match 5678 → hash(5678) % 3 = 0 → database 0
match 9012 → hash(9012) % 3 = 2 → database 2
body.say: The database is the hash of the match id modulo three. Match 1234 goes to database 1, match 5678 to database 0, and match 9012 to database 2.

body.cap: Each match id is hashed to a number, and the number modulo three picks one of the three databases.

body.x: It spreads matches evenly and needs no lookup table. The trouble starts when the number of databases changes.

items: Adding a fourth database: the code changes to % 4, and suddenly load rises on every database, not just the new one. Match 1234, which hashed to database 1 under % 3, now hashes to database 0 under % 4, and so do most other matches: almost all the data has to move. While it moves, reads are slow or fail.
Losing a database: if database 2 dies, the rule becomes % 2, and the same thing happens in reverse: almost every match changes home, not only the ones that lived on the failed database.

body.cap: Six matches on three databases. Going to % 4, or down to % 2 after a failure, moves most of them, not just the ones the change concerns.

body.x: Consistent hashing arranges both the databases and the keys on a circle of hash values, the hash ring. To keep the numbers small, imagine the ring has 100 positions, 0 to 99; real systems use the whole range of a 32-bit or 64-bit hash, 0 to 2³² − 1 or more, but the idea is the same.

items: Place the databases on the ring. With four databases, put them at 0, 25, 50 and 75.

To find a match's database, hash its id to a position and walk clockwise until you reach a database. A match at 30 belongs to the database at 50; one at 80 walks past 99 and wraps round to the database at 0.
Each database owns the arc of the ring just before it.

body.cap: Four databases at 0, 25, 50 and 75. Each match walks clockwise from its hash to the first database it meets.

body.x: Add a fifth database at position 90. Only matches whose hash falls between 75 and 90 change home: they used to walk on to the database at 0 and now stop at 90. Every other match stays exactly where it was.

body.cap: A fifth database at 90 takes over 75–90 from the database at 0. That is 15 of its 25 positions, about 15% of all matches; nothing else moves.

body.x: The database at 0 owned 25 positions (75 to 99) and hands over 15 of them, 60% of its matches, which is about 15% of all matches. With % N, adding the fifth database would have moved about 80%.
Now database 2, at position 25, fails. Only the matches it held, those hashing between 0 and 25, need a new home, and walking clockwise they now reach database 3 at 50. Everything else stays put.

body.cap: When the database at 25 fails, only its matches move, all to the next database clockwise, which now owns twice as much as the others.

body.x: But look at the result: database 3 now owns 0 to 50, twice as much as databases 1 and 4. All of the failed database's load landed on one neighbour.

The fix is to give every database many points on the ring instead of one. Hash 'DB1-vn1', 'DB1-vn2', 'DB1-vn3' and so on to get DB1's positions, and do the same for every database. The points of different databases end up mixed all around the ring.

body.cap: One point per server leaves uneven arcs, and a failed server's whole arc lands on one neighbour. Many points per server even out both.

items: When DB2 fails, the keys at 'DB2-vn1' move to whichever database comes next after that point, perhaps DB1; those at 'DB2-vn2' move to DB3; those at 'DB2-vn3' to DB4; and so on. The failed database's load is shared by all the others instead of doubling one neighbour.
When a database is added, its many points fall all around the ring, so it takes a small slice from every existing database instead of half of one neighbour's. The cluster is balanced from the start.

The more points per database, the more even it gets. Real systems use from 16 to a few hundred per server (Cassandra's default has been 16 since version 4.0, with a smarter way of placing them). Points can also be weighted, so a bigger machine gets more of them.

body.cap: With three points per database, a failed database's three arcs go to three different neighbours, so no single database doubles its load.

items: Draw the ring, place three or four servers, and show one key walking clockwise.
Show that adding a server moves only one arc, about 1/N of the keys, and that % N would move most of them.
Then add virtual nodes, and say what they fix: even arcs, and a failure spread over every server.
